authoredPrompt: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for cutting-plane angle: the learner steepens the plane through the cone, the highlighted section morphs from circle to ellipse to parabola to hyperbola, showing how one cone generates all four orbit families by changing inclination.
- Toggle between named conic cuts: the learner selects Circle, Ellipse, Parabola, or Hyperbola, the matching plane and intersection are emphasized while the others fade, clarifying which closed or open path corresponds to each slice.
authoredContext:
One of the real triumphs of Newton’s law of universal gravitation, with the force proportional to the inverse of the distance squared, is that when it is combined with his second law, the solution for the path of any satellite is a conic section. Every path taken by m is one of the four conic sections: a circle or an ellipse for bound or closed orbits, or a parabola or hyperbola for unbounded or open orbits. These conic sections are shown in the figure.

All motion caused by an inverse square force is one of the four conic sections and is determined by the energy and direction of the moving body.

A cone and its conic sections is shown. At the top a horizontal cut is shaded and a dashed line shown across the shading. This section is labeled circle. Below this a diagonal cut and line are shown. The line and cut intersect the sides of the cone. This section is labeled ellipse. Next is a diagonal cut and line that intersect the sides and the bottom of the cone and are labeled parabola. The last section is a vertical line and shaded cut labeled hyperbola

If the total energy is negative, then 0≤e<1, and the equation represents a bound or closed orbit of either an ellipse or a circle, where e=0. [You can see from the equation that for e=0, r=α, and hence the radius is constant.] For ellipses, the eccentricity is related to how oblong the ellipse appears. A circle has zero eccentricity, whereas a very long, drawn-out ellipse has an eccentricity near one.

discrepancies: Parabola/Hyperbola threshold is mathematically wrong: the code classifies parabola at ~26.6° tilt, but for this cone (R=1.5, H=3) the plane must be parallel to a generator, i.e. tilt ≈ 63.4° from horizontal; the 'Parabola' and 'Hyperbola' presets therefore show truncated ellipses while labeled otherwise

Source shows all four cutting planes simultaneously with separate dashed traces; the generated figure shows only one plane at a time (mitigated by preset buttons, but the comparative composition of the original is lost)
Section disc is colored grey-blue whereas the source renders cut surfaces in a darker shade of the teal cone color
An extra 'cutting plane' label is added that does not exist in the source
evaluation.notes: Cone, color palette, front-on view and stacked right-side labels match the source well, but the section-classification math is wrong: parabola/hyperbola presets and slider labels trigger while the section is still an ellipse, which misleads students.
action_items: Fix the classification threshold: parabola occurs when the plane tilt ≈ 90° − atan(R/H) ≈ 63.4° (parallel to a cone generator), not 26.6°; Hyperbola should require tilt > ≈63.4°
Update preset button angles (e.g. Ellipse ≈ 25°, Parabola ≈ 63.4°, Hyperbola ≈ 80°) so each button actually produces its named curve
Color the cutting-plane disc a darker teal to match the source instead of grey-blue, and remove the extra 'cutting plane' label
plan_action_items: Revise the plan's angle parameterization: classification must compare plane tilt from horizontal against the complement of the cone half-angle, otherwise the planned slider/presets encode incorrect mathematics
